title: Meta-analysis of mobile applications and their impact on student outcomes: Enhancing interest and intellectual abilities in physics learning
venue: EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether mobile applications improve students’ affective and cognitive outcomes in physics learning, with a particular focus on interest and intellectual abilities such as problem-solving, reflective thinking, creativity, and higher-order thinking. The authors position the study as filling a gap in the literature, noting that prior syntheses in physics mobile learning emphasized academic achievement more than broader intellectual and motivational outcomes.

The intervention studied is mobile learning in physics education, including a range of mobile application types such as Android-based learning media, mobile augmented reality systems, mobile science laboratories, m-learning management systems, QR-supported materials, and other app-based tools. The study uses meta-analysis procedures with a random-effects model and includes controlled experimental studies identified from Scopus and Web of Science through February/March 2025. Publication bias was assessed using funnel plots and the trim-and-fill method.

The meta-analysis synthesized 44 studies with a combined sample of 11,683 participants. The included populations were primarily high school students (29 studies) and university students (15 studies), drawn from multiple countries, with the largest share from Indonesia, followed by Morocco, Taiwan, Malaysia, Mexico, the Czech Republic, the USA, England, and Finland. Because the review spans multiple experimental studies and educational contexts, the overall setting is best characterized as not consistently reported across studies.

The main conclusion is that mobile applications had a strong positive overall effect on students’ interest and intellectual abilities in physics learning (reported overall effect size g = 1.72). Effects varied significantly by education level, year, intellectual outcome, mobile learning technique, publication type, database, and cultural context. Stronger effects were reported for outcomes such as divergent thinking, reflective thinking, laboratory report grades, learning gains, and problem-solving, while effects for technical skills and technology self-efficacy were not statistically significant. The authors conclude that mobile applications are broadly effective tools for enhancing engagement and cognitive development in physics education, while also recommending broader future research across databases, methods, and cultural contexts.

identified_tools.name: Mobile learning applications
identified_tools.description: Mobile-based instructional applications and learning tools delivered via smartphones, tablets, or other mobile devices for teaching and learning activities.
identified_tools.use_case: Meta-analysis of mobile learning interventions in physics education among high school and university students.

findings.finding_summary: Across 44 studies, mobile learning applications had a statistically significant, large positive overall effect on students' interest and intellectual abilities in physics learning.
findings.measure: overall interest and intellectual abilities in physics learning

findings.finding_summary: For high school students, mobile learning applications showed a positive effect on interest and intellectual abilities in physics learning.
findings.measure: interest and intellectual abilities in physics learning — high school subgroup

findings.finding_summary: For university students, mobile learning applications showed a positive effect on interest and intellectual abilities in physics learning.
findings.measure: interest and intellectual abilities in physics learning — university subgroup

findings.finding_summary: Mobile learning applications showed a positive effect on creative thinking skills in physics learning.
A strong positive effect was reported for reflective thinking ability.
Mobile learning applications had a positive effect on critical thinking skills in physics learning.
The pooled effect for diagrammatic and argumentative representation competence was positive.
The largest subgroup effect was reported for divergent thinking skills.
Mobile learning applications had a strong positive effect on grades for laboratory reports in physics learning.
The pooled effect for higher order thinking skills was positive.
For technical skills, the pooled estimate was not statistically significant because the confidence interval crossed zero.
Mobile learning applications showed a strong positive effect on learning gains in physics learning.
A positive effect was reported for learning independence.
Mobile learning applications had a positive effect on physics perseverance.
A strong positive effect was reported for problem-solving ability in physics learning.
Mobile learning applications showed a positive effect on representation ability.
The pooled effect on interest and perception was positive and high.
For technology self-efficacy, the pooled estimate was not statistically significant because the confidence interval crossed zero.

identified_tools.name: Lab4Physics
identified_tools.description: A mobile physics laboratory application used on mobile devices to support physics experimentation and measurement activities.
identified_tools.use_case: This review explicitly lists 'Lab4Physics mobile laboratory' as one of the mobile learning techniques represented in the meta-analysis of 44 studies on physics learning outcomes. It is treated as a distinct intervention category with 7 effect sizes covering 1,876 participants, and was analyzed for its effects on students’ interest and intellectual abilities in physics learning.

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that the Lab4Physics mobile laboratory intervention had a statistically significant, moderate positive effect on student interest and intellectual abilities in physics learning.

identified_tools.name: The Representational Triplet in Chemistry (RTC) Dictionary
identified_tools.description: A mobile learning dictionary/tool referred to as 'The Representational Triplet in Chemistry (RTC) Dictionary'.
identified_tools.use_case: Although the review is about physics learning, it explicitly includes 'The Representational Triplet in Chemistry (RTC) Dictionary' in its moderator table as a named mobile technique analyzed within the included studies. The review does not provide additional descriptive detail beyond naming it as a distinct intervention category.

findings.finding_summary: The review reports a statistically significant positive effect for the RTC Dictionary intervention on student interest and intellectual abilities.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed meta-analysis published in a journal and uses explicit inclusion criteria, moderator analyses, publication-bias checks, and a random-effects model. However, there are some concerns about heterogeneity and inclusion of studies without control groups, so it is a strong synthesis but not without limitations.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports a large positive pooled effect size (g = 1.72) for student interest and intellectual abilities in physics learning, well above the 0.20 threshold. Although effects vary by outcome and subgroup, the overall reported impact is substantial and positive.
